big: In 2008 the Nifty fell about 52%. Gold, priced in rupees, went up. That one year explains why a fund holds assets that do not move together, even when it makes the fund look dull in a rally.

lines: If I hold three things, only one of them can be the winner. Am I not just diluting my returns?
You give up some of the best year to avoid the worst one. Let us watch a made-up decade that borrows the shape of 2008.

alt: Three lines over ten made-up years: equity, gold and a 40, 40, 20 mix of equity, debt and gold
caps: Made-up yearly returns, shaped like 2008. Not real data. The mix is 40% equity, 40% debt, 20% gold.
Year 3: equity falls 52% while gold gains 27%, as in 2008. Debt adds 7%.
The mix dips a little and keeps going. Equity needs years to get back.
Equity ends highest but fell 52%. Gold dipped about 19% later. The mix never fell more than about 13%.

alt: Two bars comparing what is left of 100 rupees and the fall in the crash year
caps: Take ₹100 into year 3, the crash year.
All in equity, it ends at ₹48. The mix ends near ₹87.4, helped by gold's rise and debt's interest.
The mix fell about 12.6%. Equity alone fell 52%.
A smaller fall is easier to sit through, and easier to recover from.

title: What correlation can and cannot do
stops: Debt adds steady accrual when others wobble
Gold always rises when equity falls
alt: A shield with true and false statements about correlation
caps: Correlation says how much two assets move together. Low or negative helps smooth the ride.
In 2008, and again in the 2024 to 2026 gold rally, gold offset equity's swings for multi-asset investors.
But it changes with time. Gold does not rise every time equity falls.

q: In a crash year equity falls 52%, gold rises 27% and debt gains 7%. A fund holds 40% equity, 40% debt and 20% gold. What does the fund return, before costs?
opts: About -52%, because the biggest fall always sets the fund's result for the year
About -6%, the plain average of the three returns in that crash year
About -12.6%, found by weighing each asset's return by its share of the fund
About -20.8%, because only the equity part reacts and the rest stands still
why: The fund holds only 40% in equity, so the 52% fall hits 40% of it. The other parts also earned or lost.
A plain average ignores weights. Equity is 40% of the fund, not a third, so the result is lower than -6%.
0.4 times -52 is -20.8, plus 0.4 times 7 is 2.8, plus 0.2 times 27 is 5.4. The total is -12.6%.
-20.8% is the equity slice alone. Debt added 2.8 and gold added 5.4, so the total is higher than that.

q: A month arrives in which both equity and gold fall together. Which part of a multi-asset fund is still likely to add something?
opts: Debt, because its interest keeps accruing whatever happens to prices
Gold, because it moves against equity in each and every month, always
Equity, because it always recovers faster than the other two parts do
None of them, since all parts of a fund must fall when the market falls
why: Debt earns interest as time passes, so it adds steady accrual even when the other two are down. Rate moves can dent it.
No asset moves against another in every month. In this month gold fell too, which is the point of the question.
Equity is the most volatile part. It may recover, but it gives no steady addition in the month itself.
Parts of a fund move on their own drivers. Debt accrual can stay positive while equity and gold slip.

q: A client says: gold rose when equity halved in 2008, so gold will always cushion every future fall. How should you answer?
opts: Agree, since gold has behaved this way every single time the market has fallen in the past
Disagree, because gold actually fell in 2008 along with the Nifty, not rose
Say 2008 was a one-off, so nothing in it should affect how a fund is built today
It held in 2008 and in 2024 to 2026, but correlation shifts, so keep several cushions
why: No asset has cushioned every fall. In some periods gold has dipped as well, so 'always' is the weak word.
In 2008 gold rose in rupee terms. Stating the opposite would be wrong on the fact the lesson rests on.
The lesson of 2008 is the reason to hold assets that move differently. Calling it a one-off throws that away.
It credits the real pattern, then warns that correlation drifts. That is why a fund holds debt and rebalances too.

q: Portfolio A holds two equity funds. Portfolio B holds equity, debt and gold. Both earned the same average return. Which gives the smoother ride, and why?
opts: A, because two equity funds rising together makes the gains arrive faster
B, because its parts move at different times, so one part's dip is offset
Both are equal, because the same average return always means the same path
B, but only if gold ends up earning more than equity in the whole period
why: Equity funds tend to fall together as well. Moving together makes the falls bigger, not just the gains.
The ride depends on how the parts move relative to each other. Low correlation means dips partly offset.
The same average can come from a smooth path or a jagged one. The path, and the worst fall, will differ.
Gold need not beat equity for the mix to be smoother. Offsetting moves matter, not who earns the most.

pts: Low or negative correlation smooths the ride: in 2008 equity fell about 52% while gold rose in rupees.
Debt adds steady accrual when equity and gold both wobble. A fund's result is the weighted sum of its parts.
Correlation is not fixed. Gold helped in 2008 and 2024 to 2026, but it is a tendency, not a promise.
